asSun.p: The Moon rules Cancer and The Chariot is Cancer's card, so a Cancer Sun gets this one through the sign itself. What's worth knowing is that the Sun has no special standing in Cancer. It's a visitor there, neither helped nor hindered, and it takes its cues from the Moon, which owns the sign. So your will, the part of you that decides what you're for, runs on feeling. Cancer is cardinal as well, one of the four signs that open a season. People file it as the homebody sign and forget that. It moves first, especially when something it loves is under threat. Have a look at the card. A man in armour, two sphinxes he's steering without any reins, and a walled city still in view over his shoulder. He hasn't gone far from it. Most Cancer Suns I've read for go out into the world like that, and they could tell you exactly who it's for.

You decide what you're doing with your life by asking who it's for. That sounds soft and it isn't. At a family dinner where someone starts in on your sister, you're the one who puts down the fork. When a friend's been made redundant you've got three leads for them by Thursday. A Sunday with nothing planned makes you twitchy, so you end up reorganising the linen cupboard or driving an hour to see your mum, because a day with no direction feels a bit like being lost. You go after things sideways, too. You rarely announce a goal. You circle it, you get closer by degrees, and then one day people notice you've got it and wonder when that happened.

You can make a big change feel safe for the people going through it with you. Most people with a lot of drive leave everyone else behind. You bring them along. When a team has to relocate, or a family has to sell the place they grew up in, you're the one who works out who's going to struggle and makes sure the kettle and the photos go in the first box. You also have a long memory for why you started, which is rarer than drive. Five years into a hard thing, a lot of people have forgotten what it was for. You haven't, and you can remind them, usually without making a speech about it.

Because your drive is always in service of somebody, you can end up driving their lives for them. The adult child whose job applications you quietly rewrite. The partner whose diary you manage because it's easier. It comes from care, and that's what makes it hard to see, since nobody wants to be told their looking-after is a kind of steering. The other half of it is that you struggle to want anything just for yourself. A promotion is for the kids. The holiday is because your partner needs a break. If there's something you want with nobody attached to it, you probably talk yourself out of it, and the resentment from that leaks out months later over something small, like who forgot to put the bins out.

Something goes wrong and you get busy. Grief hits and you're organising the funeral, the casseroles, the cousins flying in from Perth. Overworked, you work harder and tidier. It looks impressive and it is, and underneath you haven't felt a thing yet. About a week later it catches up, usually in the body first. You get a cold, you can't sleep, you snap at someone over the dishwasher. The people close to you find this hard because you've been so capable that they stopped checking on you, and now you're upset that nobody checked. What helps is someone taking one job off you without asking, and you letting them, and then an evening at home where nobody needs anything from you.

You tend to fall for someone and then start building. Within a few months you've got a view on which suburb, whose couch stays, which family gets Christmas, and you're usually the one who says it out loud first. A lot of your pride goes into the life you make with a partner, and when it's working you're devoted and fierce about it, the one who'd take on anybody who hurt them. The trouble is pace. You can have the relationship three years down the road while they're still deciding whether they like your friends, and a steadier partner can end up feeling towed along. You might also take their wish for a night on their own as a vote against the whole plan. It rarely is. Ask where they'd like the two of you to be in a year, and hear the answer before you give yours.

You need work to be going somewhere and you need to care who it's for. Hand a Cancer Sun a clear aim and a group of people to look out for and they'll go through walls. Put the same person under a vague mission statement, in an open-plan office full of strangers, and the job gets done and that's about all. A lot of Cancer Suns end up running things without ever having wanted a title, because they were the one who kept the project alive when it wobbled. That's a real kind of leadership and it belongs on your CV. Keep an eye on how long you carry a work slight, though. A curt email from your manager can sit with you for a week, and it usually meant far less than you took from it.

At twenty, a Cancer Sun with this card often looks more timid than it is. You're still living by other people's plans, and the drive shows up mainly when someone you love is threatened. By the mid-thirties most people with this placement have had a stretch where they had to fight for themselves, an interstate move, a divorce, a business, a child, and found they were far tougher than they'd been told. That changes how you carry yourself. The fifties usually bring the question of who all this effort is for now. The kids leave or the parents need you, and I've seen a lot of Cancer Suns use that decade to go after one thing purely because they want it. It tends to suit them.

Write down one thing you want that has nobody else in it. Not for the family, not for the team, just for you. It can be small, a pottery class, a weekend alone in a town you like. Then take one concrete step towards it within seven days, a booking, a phone call, an enrolment form. If you catch yourself explaining to someone why it'll be good for them too, stop mid-sentence. It doesn't need to be.

asMoon.p: The Moon rules Cancer, and when your Moon is in Cancer it's at home, which in astrology is about as strong and easy as a planet gets. Nothing is forced. Your feelings work the way they're meant to, which mostly means fully, and in tides. The Chariot comes in because it's Cancer's card, and as a Moon card it's about how you carry all that feeling while still getting somewhere. Cancer being cardinal matters here more than people think. Cardinal signs act. So your emotions don't sit and stew, they make you do something, ring someone, drive over, clean the whole kitchen at eleven at night. Water that starts things is an unusual mix, and it's why a Cancer Moon can seem placid for weeks and then, one afternoon, hand in the notice without telling anyone first.

You need a base. It doesn't have to be grand, but it has to be yours, with your mug and the lamp you like, and you feel it in your stomach when it isn't. On holiday, the first night in a new room, you rearrange the furniture a little. A text left on read by someone close can sit in you all afternoon, and you'll go back over what you said in it more than once. You also remember everything through feeling. The smell of a certain soap takes you straight to your grandmother's bathroom. Your moods run in a rough cycle, a flat few days and then a lift, and the people you live with have probably clocked the pattern before you have.

People assume the gift of a Cancer Moon is being caring, and it is, but the rarer thing is that you recover. Because the Moon is at home here your feelings actually finish. They come in, they're very big, and then they go out again, and a few days later you're genuinely fine, which a lot of people never quite manage. You'll see it after an argument with a close friend. You cry, you say the hard thing, and then you're the one who texts first the next morning with a photo of something funny. You don't hang on to a hurt for sport. That makes you easy to make up with, and people come back to you for years because of it.

Moodiness can end up doing the steering. You don't mean it to, but the whole household learns to read your weather, and after a while everyone's arranging themselves around whether you're in a good way today. That's a lot of power for a feeling to have. The other one is nostalgia. You can love how things were so much that you resist what's in front of you, keeping a friendship on the terms it had at nineteen, or keeping a childhood bedroom exactly as it was long after the room is needed for something else. Going back over old hurts at two in the morning belongs here too, the same argument replayed with better lines, and you wake up tired and a bit raw for reasons nobody else can see.

When you're hurt or frightened your first instinct is to go home, literally. You cancel things, you shut the door, you make the food you ate as a kid. For a day or two that's exactly right. A week later, if nothing's shifted, the shell has usually thickened and you've started to believe nobody could understand anyway, so you stop saying anything. The people around you feel shut out and a bit guilty without knowing what they did. What helps is company that doesn't ask for an explanation. Someone who sits on the couch with you and watches something stupid. Water helps too, a bath, the beach, a long shower, and so does one small outing each day, even just to the shop.

You need to feel that you're someone's home and that they're yours. Nothing grand about it. They know how you take your tea, they notice when you've gone quiet at a party, and they come and stand next to you. Because the Moon is so comfortable in Cancer you tend to assume everyone feels this much, and they don't, so a partner's calm can read to you as not caring. Usually it's just a different temperature. Say what you need before the hurt has had a day to build. 'I need a hug and I don't want advice' saves a whole night of misunderstanding, and most partners are relieved to be told.

How you feel about the people shapes how you work far more than you'd like. A good team and you're tireless. One hostile colleague and you're checking the job ads by Wednesday. You do best with some kind of home base at work, your own desk, a regular shift, a routine you can rely on, and you tend to struggle with hot-desking and constant restructures. You're also the person colleagues confide in, and you often know who's leaving before the manager does. That's useful and it's tiring. Leave it at the door when you go. A small ritual helps, changing your clothes when you get home or taking the long way so the day has somewhere to drain off.

In your twenties a Cancer Moon often feels like too much. You cry at ads, you get homesick in places you chose to go, and you might have been told you're oversensitive often enough to half believe it. By thirty-five or so, most people with this Moon have built somewhere that feels like theirs, a flat, a family, a circle of friends, and the feelings stop feeling like a problem and start feeling like information. The fifties often bring a reckoning with your own parents, looking after them or grieving them, and that lands harder on you than on most. It's also when a lot of Cancer Moons finally stop apologising for how much they feel.

Keep a note on your phone for one full lunar month, about four weeks. Each night write one word for the day's mood and one word for what helped. Nothing more. At the end, read it through in one sitting and look for the pattern, which days dipped and what actually lifted them. Most Cancer Moons find two or three things that work almost every time. Put those somewhere you'll see them on a bad day.

asRising.p: Cancer was coming up over the eastern horizon when you were born, so Cancer is your whole first house and the Moon becomes your chart ruler. That's the planet that changes shape every few days, and it governs how you approach everything. The Chariot is Cancer's card, which makes it the card people meet first. Look at the driver. He's armoured, he's facing straight out at you, and the city he came from is still right there behind his shoulders. You come into a room a bit like that, with some metal on the front and home not far behind. Cancer being cardinal means you also open things. Strangers pick up quickly that you're watchful, and a bit later that you're the one who got the whole thing going.

At a party where you know nobody, you find the kitchen, or the host's dog, or the one other person standing near the wall, and you make a small base there before you go further. In a job interview you come across as more guarded than you feel, and a few interviewers have probably written 'reserved' in their notes. Then three months into the job you're the one everyone goes to. That lag is typical. You also read a room's mood before you read its people, so you can tell walking into a meeting that something's happened even when nobody's said a word. On the phone to a stranger, a new client or someone at the bank, you're often warmer than in person, because nobody can see you working out whether they're safe.

Because the Moon runs your chart, you adapt. Most rising signs have one way of walking in. You have several, and you pick the right one by feel, gentle with the nervous new neighbour, crisp with the tradesman who's trying it on. That's rarer than it sounds, since most people are busy managing their own nerves at a first meeting. You also protect people at a first meeting without thinking about it. You notice the kid hanging back at the barbecue and bring them into the game, or you step between a friend and someone who's getting too loud. You'd barely remember doing it the next day, and it's often the thing people bring up about you years later.

You test people at the door. You hold back until someone has proved they're safe, and it can take a long time, and a lot of perfectly good people give up before they get in. You can also sidestep. Asked a direct question by someone you don't know well, you go around it, change the subject, turn it back to them, and it can look evasive when really you just weren't ready. Your moods show on your face and in your posture, so a bad morning can colour a whole first meeting. Someone at a new job decides you don't like them from one flat hello, and it takes weeks to undo.

Under stress you close up fast. You get polite and brisk and hard to read, and people who've only just met you can find that a bit chilling. Pressure shows in how you walk into things, late, hesitant, letting the phone ring out. A week in, you've often stepped out of the situation altogether, taken leave, found a reason to be somewhere else. The people around you don't always know you're struggling because it looks like a change of plan. What helps is a familiar place and a familiar person, and then going back in with one small, clear first step, like answering the email you've been leaving or turning up to the meeting ten minutes early.

With Cancer rising, Capricorn falls on your seventh house, the house of partners, so the people you end up with are often steadier and drier than you are, and more obviously ambitious. You're drawn to someone who seems to have a plan. It can be a good match, since they're often short of exactly the warmth you've got plenty of. The early stage is the tricky part. You're slow to show interest because you're checking whether it's safe, and a Capricorn sort of person is slow to show it too, so two people can spend months being careful with each other. Somebody has to make the first move, and with a cardinal sign rising it may as well be you. Suggest the next date yourself, with a day and a place in it.

Aries sits on your tenth house, the house of career and public standing, so the working version of you is a lot more direct than the version people meet socially. That surprises colleagues. They get the careful, quiet one at the Christmas party and the person who says 'right, here's what we're doing' in the Monday meeting. You tend to do well where you can start things, new branches, launches, turnarounds, and less well in jobs that only ask you to maintain. Your first impression at work is usually of someone reliable and a bit closed. Let a couple of people see the other side early, over a coffee, so the directness doesn't come as a shock.

At twenty, Cancer rising often feels exposed. Strangers misread you, and you might hide behind a very particular look, the same jacket, the same fringe, for years. By the mid-thirties you usually know your own entry routine and can use it on purpose, so first meetings stop ambushing you. With Libra on the fourth house, home tends to become the place where you work out fairness and balance, and a lot of people with this rising end up making the house calm and good-looking for everyone, which settles them too. By the fifties the guard has usually come down a long way, and you're the one at the party who says hello first to the person standing on their own.

Next time you walk into a room full of people you don't know, give yourself a first job instead of a first conversation. Fill the water jug, take the coats, find the host and ask what needs doing. Cancer rising settles once it has a small role, and a role gets you past the watchful stage in about ten minutes. Then choose one person and ask them a real question about themselves, something other than what they do for a living.

asBirthCard.p: Your birth card is worked out from the date alone, with no sign involved. Add the digits of your birthdate, keep adding if the total's over 22, and you arrive at one of the Majors. Yours comes out at seven. Seven sits straight after The Lovers, the card of choosing, and just before Strength, the card of patience, so it's what happens once you've made a choice and have to act on it. It's a number of movement. Traditionally it's three plus four, the idea and the solid thing, and there are seven days in a week and seven notes in a scale, a full turn that brings you round to start again. The Chariot itself belongs to Cancer, a water sign that moves first, and that's part of the card's nature whatever your own signs happen to be.

As a pattern across a life, seven shows up as leaving and arriving. You've probably moved more than most people you know, or changed schools, or changed careers, or there was one big departure early that shaped everything after. You're at your best on the road in some sense. The first week in a new job, the drive to a new city with everything in the boot, the moment a project goes from planning to actually happening. What you find harder is the long flat stretch after arriving, the third year in the same house, when there's nothing left to push towards. Around then you'll notice yourself looking at maps, or looking for the next thing.

A seven can hold a pair of demands that pull against each other and still get somewhere. Think of the person who's caring for a sick parent and finishing a degree in the same year, and somehow passes. That's often a seven. You don't need your life to be tidy to move it forward. Because you've had to start over more than once, you're also good at helping other people through a change. The friend who's just split up and has to find a flat, the colleague starting in a new country, they end up on your couch with a spreadsheet, and they're sorted by the end of the evening.

Movement can turn into a way of never landing. Every time something gets difficult, a relationship that needs work, a job that's gone stale, you feel the pull to move on and call it progress. Sometimes it is. Sometimes it's the old pattern, and you've swapped the scenery without changing anything. The other trap is winning. Sevens tend to rack up victories and get attached to them, so an argument with your brother over who's driving becomes something that has to be won. You might notice you go oddly flat the week after a win, too, and start looking for the next one before you've told anyone about this one.

When things go badly, a seven's first move is almost always to move. You book the trip, you apply for the transfer, you start the renovation. Doing something big makes you feel in control again. A week or so later, if the problem came with you, which it usually does, you get tired and a bit short with people, and the ones who helped you pack are confused about why you're still miserable. What actually helps is staying put long enough to find out what the trouble was. One conversation, in one place, before you change anything else. Then move if you still need to.

Love for a seven tends to come in chapters, and each one has usually arrived with a move or a big change attached. You often meet people on the way somewhere, at a new job, in a new city, on a trip. The pattern to watch is choosing people who come with a project, someone to rescue or a situation to overcome, because that gives the relationship somewhere to go. When the project's done, you can find the ordinary stretch hard. The relationships that last for sevens usually have a shared aim in them, a house to build, a business, a garden, something the two of you are working at together.

Sevens do well in work that goes somewhere visible. Logistics, sport, sales, emergency work, project management, anything with a start line and a finish line and some resistance in between. You like a clear target and you like people to know you hit it. What doesn't suit you is a job where success is invisible or endless, maintenance forever with no milestone. If you're stuck in one, carve it into stages yourself and tick each one off. And watch how you treat colleagues when you're chasing a deadline. The push that gets the thing done can run straight over the quiet person who's been doing the careful work.

A seven at twenty is usually in a hurry. Lots of starts, lots of energy, and not much patience for anyone telling you to wait. By the mid-thirties most sevens have had at least one big win and at least one crash, and the crash usually teaches them to check where they're headed before they put their foot down. That's when the steering improves. You go after fewer things and actually finish them. In the fifties the pattern often turns towards Strength, the card after yours, and a lot of sevens find they're content to hold a place and look after it. They still move, just more slowly and with more say over where they're going.

Before your next big change, a move, a new job, a new start of any kind, write down three things. What you're moving towards, what you're moving away from, and what's coming with you whether you like it or not. Keep the list somewhere you'll find it. Six months after the change, get it out and read it, and spend the longest on the third one. That's usually the one that tells you whether the move fixed anything.
